indie-rock.d: Rock released on self-run labels outside the major-label system: guitar-led, roughly recorded, with a detached attitude that later became the mother lode of all alternative music.

jangle-pop.d: Bright, echoing Rickenbacker guitars ring out; The Smiths and R.E.M. made it the standard 80s indie guitar tone.

twee-pop.d: Deliberately childish, sweetly melodic indie pop: hand drums, childlike harmonies, lyrics about crushes and bicycles; Belle and Sebastian are the archetype.

c86.d: NME's cassette compilation named a whole generation of UK indie bands: noisy yet sweet, DIY, strongly live-sounding; early Primal Scream were among them.

britpop.d: Britain's 90s answer to grunge: Beatlesque melody, working-class narratives and media wars; Oasis and Blur defined it.

madchester.d: Manchester wired indie guitars to acid house drum machines and dancefloor grooves; Stone Roses and Happy Mondays were the flagships.

baggy.d: Madchester's looser offshoot: heavier funk bass, more casual clothes and moves, directly connecting to the later Britpop.

dream-pop.d: Voices and guitars wrapped in reverb and delay, like hearing songs through fog; Cocteau Twins and Beach House share the same temperature thirty years apart.

noise-pop.d: Pop melodies wrapped in walls of noise; The Jesus and Mary Chain's Psychocandy was the watershed.

indie-pop.d: Pop released on independent labels: melody first, light-touch production, sitting between twee and mainstream pop.

bedroom-pop.d: Pop finished in a bedroom with a laptop and one microphone: lo-fi, intimate, very wet reverb, the new indie of the streaming era.

surf-rock.d: California surf culture set to reverb guitars: tremolo, glissando and fast picking; Dick Dale's Misirlou is the ultimate template.

garage-punk.d: Garage rock's rawness meets punk's energy: distortion, shouting, three chords; The Stooges are the prototype.

space-rock.d: Long repetitive passages, synthesizers and echo create a sense of weightlessness; Hawkwind blazed the trail and Spacemen 3 made it more minimal still.

noise-rock.d: Atonality, feedback and structural breakdown brought into rock; Sonic Youth and Big Black made it the underground language of 80s New York and Chicago.

slowcore.d: Rock slowed to near stillness: slow tempos, silence and hushed voices; Low and Codeine build pressure out of quiet.

post-grunge.d: Grunge's distortion and attitude sanded down into radio-friendly rock; Foo Fighters and Nickelback dominated the whole 2000s.

j-rock.d: Japan's localised take on rock: high melodic density, anime and visual kei culture; X Japan were the late-80s peak.

rock-en-espanol.d: Rock sung in Spanish: from Argentina to Mexico, translating Anglo-American rock into Latin American politics and youth.

pop-rock.d: Rock instrumentation handed over to pop melody: clear choruses, three-minute lengths; the backbone of 70s radio.

soft-rock.d: Rock's electric edge turned down and its melodies softened: piano, harmonies and adult balladry; Fleetwood Mac are the model.

arena-rock.d: Rock written for tens of thousands to sing along: huge choruses, guitar solos, fireworks and stadiums; Journey and Bon Jovi are typical.

southern-rock.d: The rock of the American South: twin guitars, blues roots, long improvisations; Lynyrd Skynyrd's Free Bird is the anthem.

art-rock.d: Treating rock as an art project: concepts, theatricality, non-pop structures; David Bowie and Roxy Music turned it into a stance.

bubblegum-pop.d: Three-minute sweets built for teenagers: simple choruses, cartoonish production; The Archies' Sugar, Sugar sold six million copies.

adult-contemporary.d: Soft pop designed for radio's office-hours slot: piano, strings, non-threatening love; Carpenters are the template.

europop.d: Continental European pop: disco rhythms, synthesizers and choruses that stick; ABBA exported it to the whole world.

cantopop.d: Hong Kong's Cantonese pop: TV theme songs, the idol industry and localised Japanese melodies; Leslie Cheung and Anita Mui are the golden age.

jpop.d: The catch-all for Japanese pop: from kayōkyoku to idols and Shibuya-kei, dense melodies and polished arrangements; Hikaru Utada carried it into the million-selling era.

mandopop.d: Mandarin-language pop: campus folk, ballads and R&B-inflected production; Jay Chou brought rhythm and rap into the Chinese-language mainstream.

afropop.d: The global 2010s face of Afrobeats: Nigerian melody, Ghanaian highlife guitar and dance rhythms; Wizkid took it into the UK and US charts.

power-pop.d: Beatlesque melody plus distorted guitars and tight drumming: the chorus must grab you at once; Big Star were the commercially unsung gods.

art-pop.d: Pop as an experimental playground: unconventional structures, theatrical singing and visual concepts; Kate Bush and Björk are the exemplars.
